slides.title: A thread is work with a lifetime
slides.eyebrow: A THREAD IS WORK WITH A LIFETIME
keyPoints: Creation can start execution immediately
Shared objects must outlive access
Completion needs an owning join policy
slides.narration: Starting a thread creates a new execution stream that may begin before the creator reaches its next statement. Prepare every referenced object first. The creator also needs a policy for collecting the work, even if a later setup step throws. A thread handle is therefore more than a launch button: it represents a lifecycle obligation. C++20 jthread helps by requesting stop and joining during destruction when appropriate. That does not force a blocked worker to finish or keep an already-destroyed captured object alive. Design the worker's inputs, owner, stop condition, and join point together before testing its result.
actions: Ask learners to predict the specific result before revealing it.
Trace the state and lifetime rule that supports the answer.

question.prompt: Can initialization placed immediately after launching a worker be assumed to happen first?
question.answer: No. The worker may run immediately; referenced shared state must be prepared before launch or protected by an explicit protocol.

slides.title: Capture identity by value and storage by reference
slides.eyebrow: CAPTURE IDENTITY BY VALUE AND STORAGE BY REFERENCE
keyPoints: A copied task index stays distinct
Referenced output storage stays owned by the caller
Joining precedes every parent read
slides.narration: A loop that launches workers has two different kinds of data. The task index identifies which job this worker should do, so each worker needs its own copied value. The result array is shared storage owned by the parent, so each worker can borrow a reference if the array outlives the work. Capturing the changing loop index by reference may make all workers use the same final value and may introduce conflicting access. The repair is not a lucky delay. Capture the intended identity by value and give each worker a distinct output slot, then join before the parent reads those slots.

Trace the state and lifetime rule that supports the answer.

question.prompt: Why should the loop index be copied even when the result array is borrowed?
question.answer: The index is a per-task identity that must not change with the loop; the array is longer-lived storage deliberately shared in disjoint slots.

slides.title: Run workers whose identities cannot drift
slides.eyebrow: RUN WORKERS WHOSE IDENTITIES CANNOT DRIFT
keyPoints: Three copied indexes select three slots
Each worker writes one separate element
Leaving the owner scope joins all workers
slides.narration: The loop creates three jthreads. The capture list takes id by value and results by reference. Each worker stores ten plus its own index into one distinct array element. The vector of thread owners lives in an inner scope, so leaving that scope joins the workers before printing. The output is 10 11 12 even if worker two finishes first. Distinct ordinary array elements are separate locations for this access pattern, and no worker resizes the array. The example does not promise a particular launch order or performance gain. Its result follows from stable identities, separate writes, sufficient storage lifetime, and the join boundary.

question.prompt: What ensures results is still alive while the workers use it?
question.answer: It is declared outside the thread-owner scope, and all jthread owners join before that outer array is read or destroyed.

slides.title: A worker exception needs an explicit channel
slides.eyebrow: A WORKER EXCEPTION NEEDS AN EXPLICIT CHANNEL
keyPoints: Catch inside the thread callable
Store an exception_ptr while the parent waits
Rethrow only after joining
slides.narration: An exception escaping an ordinary C++ thread function does not automatically travel to its creator. This example catches the failure inside the worker and stores an exception_ptr, a handle to the captured exception. Main joins before inspecting that handle, so the worker's write and the parent's read are ordered. Rethrowing in main reaches the normal catch and prints caught: bad sample. The demonstration uses one writer and a join, so it does not need a mutex for concurrent handle access. A design that inspects failures while workers continue would need another synchronization rule. Error transport, like result transport, must be part of the thread contract.

question.prompt: Why is reading failure after join safe without a mutex in this specific program?
question.answer: Only the worker writes the handle, main waits for its completion, and main reads afterward with the join synchronization relationship.

A thread normally terminates by returning from its callable. An uncaught exception escaping a C++ thread function causes termination of the program under the standard thread interface; it is not automatically delivered to the creating thread. slides.title: Shared address spaces
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: Threads can access the same globals, heap objects, and explicitly shared stack objects.
Shared addressability does not imply permission to perform unsynchronized conflicting operations.
Ordinary mutable state needs ownership or synchronization.
Read-only data is simpler, but its initialization must be safely published and its lifetime maintained.
slides.narration:
Threads can access the same globals, heap objects, and explicitly shared stack objects. Shared addressability does not imply permission to perform unsynchronized conflicting operations. Ordinary mutable state needs ownership or synchronization. Read-only data is simpler, but its initialization must be safely published and its lifetime maintained. A pointer to immutable bytes is still unsafe after the owner destroys or reallocates the storage.

In plain English: Think of an address written on a note: the note can tell you where to look, but it does not prove the thing is still there or that you are allowed to use it.

keyPoints: Thread-local state gives each thread a distinct instance, reducing accidental sharing.

Thread-local storage also consumes resources per thread, so a design with enormous thread counts can multiply memory costs.

slides.title: Independent partial sums
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: Four workers sum disjoint ranges of the integers 1 through 100.
Each writes a distinct array element.
The parent combines results only after the worker owners leave scope and join.
Companion listing: ch44/partial_sums.cpp
slides.narration: Four workers sum disjoint ranges of the integers 1 through 100. Each writes a distinct array element. The parent combines results only after the worker owners leave scope and join. Companion listing: ch44/partial_sums.cpp The expected result is 5050. There is no conflicting access to the same array element during worker execution, and joining completes before the parent’s reads. Adjacent elements may still share a cache line, so the design can exhibit false sharing in a more write-intensive workload without containing a language-level data race. This example demonstrates correctness, not useful speedup for 100 additions. Thread creation overhead is likely to dominate such a small workload. A performance experiment should reuse workers or use sufficiently large tasks while preserving the same partitioning argument.

slides.title: Join means completion and an ordering guarantee
slides.eyebrow: JOIN MEANS COMPLETION AND AN ORDERING GUARANTEE
keyPoints: The worker can finish before join is called
join still collects the completed thread
Post-join reads observe the completed work
slides.narration: A join is useful even when the worker has already returned. It collects the thread's completion and supplies the synchronization relationship needed for the parent's later reads. It is not merely a request to wait a certain number of milliseconds. In our array example, no parent read occurs until every worker owner has joined. Replacing that boundary with a sleep would remove the proof because scheduling can delay a worker beyond the guessed duration. Conversely, joining immediately after every launch may make intended parallel work run one worker at a time. Choose the completion boundary according to the data dependency, not simply the next convenient line.
actions: Ask learners to predict the specific result before revealing it.
Trace the state and lifetime rule that supports the answer.

question.prompt: Why can joining each worker immediately after launch defeat overlap?
question.answer: The creator waits for each worker to finish before launching the next, serializing work that could otherwise be independent.

slides.title: Automatic joining cannot solve an impossible wait
slides.eyebrow: AUTOMATIC JOINING CANNOT SOLVE AN IMPOSSIBLE WAIT
keyPoints: jthread destruction requests stop and joins
Workers must observe a supported stop protocol
Do not join while holding a mutex the worker needs
slides.narration: Imagine a worker waiting for a queue to close, while its owner destroys a jthread without first closing the queue. Automatic joining now waits for a worker that has no reason to return. A stop request helps only if the worker checks it or uses a wait integrated with that request. Another trap is destroying the thread owner while holding a mutex the worker needs to finish. The owner waits for the worker, and the worker waits for the owner to release the lock. Scope design must release locks and establish shutdown conditions before joining. Resource cleanup order is part of the progress proof.

question.prompt: Why can a correctly owned jthread still hang during destruction?
question.answer: Its worker may wait forever or need a resource held by the joining thread; ownership does not itself establish a termination path.

slides.title: Stack location does not prevent sharing
slides.eyebrow: STACK LOCATION DOES NOT PREVENT SHARING
keyPoints: A reference can expose a stack object
Lifetime and access rules still apply
Per-thread stacks multiply resource costs
slides.narration: A local variable usually lives in one thread's stack frame, but another thread can access it if given a pointer or reference. The word local describes declaration scope, not a magical barrier against sharing. If the frame ends while the worker still uses the reference, the worker has a lifetime error even if only one thread writes. Separately, thousands of threads can reserve substantial stack resources, and large local arrays or deep recursion increase pressure. A thread-per-request design needs a resource budget as well as a synchronization plan. Sometimes a bounded worker pool is easier to control than an unbounded number of individually simple workers.

question.prompt: Does a pointer to another thread’s local object keep that object alive?
question.answer: No. The owner must keep the object’s lifetime open through every use, typically by joining before its scope ends.

slides.title: Thread-local data reduces sharing but needs collection
slides.eyebrow: THREAD-LOCAL DATA REDUCES SHARING BUT NEEDS COLLECTION
keyPoints: Each thread has a distinct instance
Global totals need an explicit aggregation phase
Resource use grows with thread count
slides.narration: A thread_local counter gives each thread its own instance, so updates do not all contend for one shared counter. That does not automatically provide a global result. The program needs a collection phase while the relevant values still exist, or workers can return ordinary partial results to an owner. Thread-local initialization and destruction follow thread lifetime rather than one function call, which matters in a reused worker pool. Cached state can survive from one task to another unless deliberately reset. Use thread-local storage for a clear per-thread requirement, and account for its memory cost multiplied by the number of workers.

question.prompt: Why can thread-local state surprise a program that reuses worker threads?
question.answer: The state can persist across multiple tasks on the same thread, so task-specific assumptions require resetting or a different storage lifetime.
